utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Case IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, there are a few things we can sort out before we start the evidence this morning. First, there is some problem about the protective measures, I gather, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness, the witness 71, has obviously misunderstood the possibilities and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I can understand that there could be mistakes, but we seem to be getting an awful lot of them. Who is responsible for the protective measures applications? Is it the investigators or is it the team?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's the investigators and the language assistants who always talk with the witnesses, but because of the language issue, there may be problems in this regard. That caused this witness to misunderstand the situation and he thought he could only ask image distortion or pseudonym and not both together, and so that is how the confusion started here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, have you got any problem with adding the pseudonym, by which we've known him anyway all through the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. We do not have any objections, and I really see not much purpose in saying it because requests for applications for protection always arrive at the very last moment, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, the next matter is this --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is just another -- I'm very embarrassed now, but it's another witness who also asked in the last minute protective measures, and that is the Witness 15, who comes next. This witness did not request any protective measures at all and now he requests image alteration because he has property in Foca and intends to go there and take care of the matter in Foca, and he's concerned that if his face is published, he may be placed under some risk from individuals with nationalistic resentments. And he also requested it only now during the conference here with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, he seeks only facial distortion?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, only facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You say he's the next witness. He's the third witness in the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. It's number 15, witness number 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Bakrac, you will complain, I know, and you will have justification for complaining about it being late, but what about the merits?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing, Your Honour, nothing new. All witnesses seem to be protected, either their faces or their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. In relation to FWS-71, we will amend the order for protective measures to add that he shall use the pseudonym FWS-71. For FWS-15, we will order protective measures that his face -- he be given facial distortion. It always sounds a little grim. Now, the next matter is this videolink. We have now got your additional material, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. This is for the witness that both sides want called. Has there been anything further that you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll handle this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. There's nothing to add to what we filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What's your attitude about that one, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. If I understand, it's (redacted) RJ. Is that him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence agreed with the examination of this witness and we also intended to call him. But on the basis of the information that we received in the motion and after talking to the accused, we realised - and from what we received from the Prosecutor - we understand that the doctor is worried about this witness' testimony - that is, testimony as such, not coming here to The Hague and appearing before the Chamber or by videolink but the testimony itself - because it will bring back memories of that time, and this might impair his health. That is why we are not insisting to call the witness. And we repeat: Yes, the Defence would like to have that witness examined. We spoke to the accused. The accused knows the witness. They worked together. But from what we were told by the Prosecutor, we concluded that the fact of testimony itself might prejudice his health, and that is why we decided to insist on examining this witness, and that includes both the protection that was requested and the videolink conference. We do not object against the videolink. With regard to the videolink, we have our principled attitude that you know about, but in view of the state of the witness' health and that the fact of testimony could prejudice his health further, we think that this witness should not be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand the stand you take. What the Prosecution is seeking is to have him give evidence, but by way of videolink and in a closed Court, so that when his evidence is being brought to the Tribunal by way of videolink it will be a closed Court here and nobody else will see it. The witness himself has said that he wants to give evidence, but apparently he seems to understand that if he's allowed to give it in his hometown, his health should not suffer as much as it would if he had travelled. Now, when you say you don't want him called, do you mean you don't want him called here or you don't want him to give evidence at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we understand and we do not have any objections against videolink testimonies or in a closed session, but from what we received from the Prosecution, the Defence and the accused understand that the testimony as such, in whatever form, by videolink or his appearance before the Court, might affect his health. That is how we understood what the Prosecution gave us and from their application to the Chamber. And we are concerned about this. We do not want his testimony to affect his health, and that is why the Defence does not insist on examining this witness; that is, it doesn't really matter whether the witness will be coming here or testifying by videolink. From what we have received from the Prosecution, we understood that any -- whatever form his testimony took, it could nevertheless affect his health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think I'll have to ask you for a specific answer to yes or no. Are you objecting to his evidence being received by the Tribunal in any way?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we do not object against his testimony in whatever form, but we believe we were duty-bound because the order said that the Defence was requesting the testimony of this witness. The Defence does not insist anymore on calling this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. We'll note that you no longer insist, but you don't object to the videolink or to the closed Court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. All right. Well, then the Trial Chamber will make the order sought in the motion. When is it likely -- is it going to be today that we have this witness? It's again you, Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In discussions with the technical people, we understand they need two weeks, so this witness will probably have to -- we would ask that the summons be altered so the date is changed, but we'll arrange a date and file an additional motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll make the order without a date and make it for a date to be fixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Now, is that all the housekeeping matters we have to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From the Prosecution side, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything that you want to raise, Mr. Bakrac? You have promised us a few things: Photographs from the various rooms; you are to state whether the materials which are presently identified as P55/2 may be admitted into evidence; and you were going to tell us where the Defence has taken issue with the Prosecution case that the Muslim prisoners received less food than the Serb prisoners. So there are three things there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as regards the photographs, we went to the place and we've brought the photographs and are waiting -- and then had them developed. However, the shots of some rooms have failed, so we'll have to do that again. But another matter, and that is in Room 20 [as interpreted], what we had mostly challenged here, that was Room 23 and view from there, and I have these photographs, but the Defence will keep them and will show them to witnesses when the matter arises of what the witness could see from that room and what he couldn't. If I'm wrong, if that is not how things should be, then I will produce the photographs and show them. As for Exhibit 55/2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let's deal with them one at a time. You have an obligation under the Rules to put those photographs to any witness the Prosecution calls who says that they can see something on the bridge, so that you would have to put it to the witnesses, whoever is called, who give that evidence. It may be the Prosecution will want to recall some witnesses - I don't know - once they've seen the photographs. But that's your obligation. If you think that it may save time, it would be perfectly appropriate for you to show the photographs to the Prosecution. You're not obliged to. But certainly the first witness that now is called who gives evidence of what they saw in relation to the bridge from somewhere on the top floor of the KP Dom, then you are obliged to show them these photographs so they can deal with them. Now, the second matter, P55/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe I said so. I have nothing as regards photographs. We can show them to the Prosecutor, we can show them to the Chamber, and whichever witness tackles the matter, we shall be showing them. As for the second matter, we do not object against the admission of Exhibit P55/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The next matter is where the Defence has taken issue with the Prosecution case that the Muslim prisoners received less food than the Serb prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies but the Defence was concerned with presenting its case when it starts, presents without any delays, so that we seized the opportunity given us by this break to go to the ground, speak to witnesses, see which one of them -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which ones of them are seeking protective measures and whatnot, and we spent all the time on the ground. But until we establish if this should be challenged, the Defence will, at its own risk, in the course of this week, check once again the transcripts, from the first to the last witness, and if we come across a situation where this is challenged, then we shall approach the bench, the Court, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, it's probably a very long time since I was counsel appearing in a case, but I have never forgotten the amount of work which counsel has to do in order to keep up with the trial, so I understand completely myself the problems you've had in seeing your witnesses, and I would not expect you to do this task or undertake this task whilst you're getting ready to cross-examine witnesses during the week. But I think that with Friday off and the weekend off, by next Monday we must have those transcript references because we are trying desperately to keep the issues which are -- the matters which are in issue identified, and it's sometimes a little hard. So we will give you until next Monday for that. Is there anything else you want to raise now that we are back at work? When I say "back at work," back at work on this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much for your understanding. Rest assured we shall do it by next week. We do not have any other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, we will have to have the blinds lowered to bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but Your Honours, I think there is one matter open still and I thought it would be addressed but it was not. When we heard the evidence of Ms. Manas, we talked about the rubble in front of the KP Dom being part of the Aladza mosque and the defence counsels wanted to check if this is conceded or if we need to have a historian here to testify. And I thought this was also sought out last week by Defence counsel. That is at least my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I confess I had overlooked that because I had put those photographs away in the exhibit folder instead of my court folder. Have you discussed this matter, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before the break we discussed it, and he said he would go to Foca and find out and give his opinion on this today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And you have not had any response directly from him?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bakrac, what about the rubble?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I expected the OTP to raise the matter and that is why I did not bring it up. Yes, my learned friend is quite correct. We spent the whole break on the ground going into all these matters, and we do not challenge, that is we do not have any -- we are not objecting against admitting this documentation as evidence and confirming that these are indeed the remains of the Aladza mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I was waiting for this to be interpreted but since we are talking about various issues, and my learned friend has reminded me, we also talked about a witness for whom -- the witness is 05. That witness is very important for the Defence and it was mentioned that we would find a way to have him testify, either by videolink or in some other way. We discussed it with the OTP before the 15th of January. That is at the beginning of the last session, which began on the 15th of January. We still have not heard from the OTP what they think about the testimony of Witness 05. If you remember, the Prosecution applied for the introduction of documents through this witness but these documents were introduced or presented through another witness, and when I objected, you said, Your Honour, that those documents had nothing to do with Witness 05 and therefore could not serve as exhibits along with Witness 05, and we still have not heard from the Prosecution but we insist on calling Witness 05, because in his statement, he said something which is of great relevance for the solution of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I won't deny that I said something about documents but I have absolutely no recollection. I remember there was a discussion about the difficulties in getting FWS-05. Well, what is the situation of 05, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I met the witness recently and he is in a very bad shape so he will not -- we will not go for him the videolink testimony. We would rather drop the witness. But I think we should discuss it further with the Defence counsel if we have other ways to get his testimony in. We were actually thinking about a 92 bis proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I know what 92 bis is. I was thinking of a -- depositions are 71, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. We were actually thinking of putting in his statement as he gave, as a document, like a 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, 94, yes, one of the new ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we were thinking. But the problem is it's, of course, not in the form that it needs to be, but 94 bis (C) allows for putting in other statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But 92 bis -- it is 92 bis, you are right, but there, of course, it would be subject to cross-examination if the Defence requests it and we order it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So it may not cure the problem. But if there is some document that can be proved only through this witness, there may be some agreement about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We were actually thinking about using 92 bis (C), that is a written statement not in a form as prescribed by paragraph B may be admissible but, however, the threshold for using, let's say, an ICTY statement is quite high. It says: Subsequently died or no longer with reasonable diligence be traced or by reason of bodily or mental conditions unable to testify orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is also a very important part of it, that the Trial Chamber must be satisfied that the circumstances in which the statement was made and recorded, there are satisfactory indicia of its reliability.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and we therefore thought we rather drop the witness altogether, including the documents that he could provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And that, too is subject to (E), as I understand it, that we may do so only if the witness appears for cross-examination if we are satisfied that it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So you have a number of things, but may we leave that one perhaps for counsel to discuss?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not very convenient to be dealing with it in court, and we will come back to that. I don't remember which document it was that was the problem. Well, then, the document which is presently marked for identification P55/2 will be Exhibit P55/2. Were those photographs that we were given of the rubble admitted into evidence or were they merely given a number?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: They were admitted into evidence. It was just kept open what relevance they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see. Right. Thank you very much. All right. Well, the matter that is yet to be determined is that relating to FWS-05. Can we have the witness now? The pseudonyms document headed FWS-71 will be Exhibit P426 and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in the document which has been handed to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, sir. And we apologise for having kept you waiting whilst we were dealing with some other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have in front of you a sheet of paper with the number 71, FWS-71 on it, yes?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour I apologise for interrupting my learned colleague but the witness just took out yet another piece of paper where it says something, and the Defence doesn't know what this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you know what it is, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness had some notes for his memory, to help his memory, but I would rather think he should put them away. I don't think that he would need them now, and if the matter arises we could come back to what he has pulled out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Please, I would like to put a question. Notes can be made available to the opposing party as well. There is nothing secretive in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If you feel that you need to refer to the notes, then a copy will have to be given to the Defence, but I suggest you put them away for the moment. If you need to use them, by all means, say so. Before you start Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I would like some assistance from the booth. My laptop is not operating. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you get underway.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, your number 71 is your pseudonym. You were granted your request for a pseudonym. When you look at the sheet in front of you, there is a name under the number 71. Is it your name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, that's my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the date next to the name, is it your birth date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. The date is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on this sheet you also find a lot of other names and pseudonym numbers, so in case you want to refer to these witnesses, please say the number and not the name. Witness, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I was born in Danicici, in the municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you have children? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. Two.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you live before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I lived in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which part of the town?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: The centre of town, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it a house or did you live in an apartment building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: It was an apartment building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What profession do you have?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you work before the war? And please do not tell us your exact position, just your office.

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I worked in the employment office of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the Foca office.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In your work, did you get to know many citizens of Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: My job made it possible for me to meet quite a few citizens of Foca, and I did know quite a few citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "quite a few," what do you mean? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, I can give you a very approximate percentage, but let's say that I knew 75 to 80 per cent of the population of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you a member of any of the newly formed political parties?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you involved in politics before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: The former League of Communists, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But in the years 1991, 1992, were you involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the war broke out in Foca, did you participate in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the war started, where were you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I was in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you leave Foca after the --

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you leave?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: On the 12th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did you leave?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Because that part of town had been free of war danger.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did anyone suggest to you to leave the town?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. Suggested and helped.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And without saying the name, who was that, from ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: A Serb, my next-door neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why did he suggest to you to leave?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Because we were together in premises where it became obvious that the situation was such that nobody could guarantee anybody's life, and the Serbs had already taken a part of town; actually, that part of town where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did this person help you out of Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you need this help of a Serb neighbour or could you have gone without any help?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: It was absolutely necessary, because I had no other way out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why was it necessary for -- was it necessary for anybody or was it necessary for Muslims to get help by their Serbian neighbours?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Absolutely all Muslims required the help of their Serb neighbours, those who happened to be in that part of town that was falling at the time of the fall of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why, and what kind of help?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Help in terms of getting out there and saving your life, because your life was jeopardised. The soldiers were already in town, of course, with rifles in their hands. What else could you expect but death?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I went to Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you arrested while you were in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: On the 21st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What time of the day did it happen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: In the morning, around 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I was asleep in a room at the place of this man where I was staying.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in what town in Montenegro were you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: The town of Bar, the neighbourhood of Pecurice.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: The police of the Bar MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what happened on that morning? How did this happen, this arrest?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: A police patrol came, three or four policemen. They came in a police vehicle. One of them came into the room where we were asleep and he called out my name, as well as the name of two of my neighbours who were staying there with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The two neighbours, who were they? Can you tell us the names and their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. (redacted). They're also Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were they also from Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These policemen, did they tell you why you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: We were just told that we would be taken for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you illegally in Montenegro, or do you know why you were taken for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: The first day I arrived in Montenegro, I had to register with the police authorities and the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How was the atmosphere towards Muslims in Bar? The local population, how did they treat you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: During the first ten days one couldn't notice anything. However, on one occasion when I was at the Red Cross, I came for some aid. One could feel certain provocations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of provocations and why were there provocations?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, first by the employees of the Red Cross, those of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they accuse you of anything? Did they -- why were there these resentments? What caused it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, actually, they kept saying to us, "This is not an institution for you. This is for our Serb brothers."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were you taken when you were arrested? To which place?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: We were taken to the police station in Bar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Besides the three of you that you mentioned, were there other persons arrested and taken to the police station in Bar?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. The police station in Bar, in a big room there, I found Kubat Sefko and Redzo Sacir tied to chairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: They were citizens of Foca, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any officials from Foca in the police station in Bar?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Miodrag Stevanovic, nicknamed Mico.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, nicknamed Sumar. Yes, I knew him from before.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was he doing in Bar, in the police station?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He was in charge of arresting people all over Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know that at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, I knew on that day, when I was brought to the police station, because I saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But his authority to arrest people all over Montenegro, did you know that already at that time or did you learn that later on?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Later, absolutely. That's when I found out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how did you find out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I found out later at the MUP in Herceg-Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did you -- what did you find out there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I found out from people who had also been arrested and who were staying in the area of Herceg-Novi who were put up as refugees there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was Mr. Stevanovic wearing when you saw him in Bar and later?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, of course he was wearing jeans and some kind of a leather jacket.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you speak with him in Bar at the police station? Did he interrogate you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did anyone else from your -- from the other people arrested, from the other Muslims, did anyone else speak with him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who, and what was said? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Redzo Sacir and Cerimovic, Ibrahim had the opportunity of talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they tell you what he had said?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Redzo Sacir told us who was down there as soon as he came back and why he had come.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And why? What did Redzo learn from Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He introduced himself as a MUP inspector, as an inspector with the Foca MUP. He said that he came with the intention of talking to people from Foca who were in the territory of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he say anything else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I think he did say something in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he tell you why you were arrested or did he tell the other two gentlemen you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Are you referring to the arrest in Montenegro, whether he told me about it on the spot or some other occasion?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, on the spot. Did you learn on the spot why you were arrested, either from him or from your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes. We were absolutely told that we were arrested, because there was such propaganda over Radio Montenegro and the other media that in Montenegro there were Green Berets that had appeared, the so-called balijas.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Green Berets, what would that mean? What is that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: At that time I didn't know either. I guess these were some kind of armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know. A platoon, unit, whatever you call it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you later meet Mr. Stevanovic in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him within the compound of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did he tell you anything on this occasion when you met him in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he had to do what he did, it was sort of, "What could I do about it?" Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did he tell you who ordered him to arrest you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever find out why you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, I never found out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you interrogated in Bar or later on, on your way, in Herceg Novi?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No. I was never interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the police station in Bar, how many Muslims were taken there and detained there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Twenty-one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In Bar, already in Bar? It's not enough to nod. You have to say yes or no, because we have to have it on --

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, 21. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were also Serbs arrested, Serbs from Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: That happened in Herceg Novi, when we were transferred from Bar to Herceg Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Bar in the police station?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: From the 21st until the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you were taken to the police station in Herceg Novi. Were all Muslims kept in Bar taken to Herceg Novi?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, no. I was taken to Herceg Novi on the 25th of May -- sorry, the 24th of May. There was a group of 21 persons who were brought to the police station in Bar. They singled out me, Kameric, Abdulah; Babic, Ramiz; Kubat Sefko. That was the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why were you singled out? Does that mean the other Muslims were released in Bar?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. The others were set free. I don't know why they singled out the persons whose names I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Herceg Novi?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: From the 24th until the 25th, two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where were you taken from there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: At 3.00 on the 25th, we were put onto a bus together with 25 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many Muslims were on the bus?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Twenty-one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did they come from? Were all of you from Foca or also from other areas in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No. We were not all from Foca, there were also people from Srebrenica, Gorazde, Sarajevo, Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And these 25 Serbs, where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I personally did not know them. These were people who were from the territory of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know why they were arrested and taken to Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, they were arrested because they thought that they had fled the war, and then they wanted to return them so that they would go to the front line, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who escorted you to the border? Who was on the bus and were there any other vehicles accompanying you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: On the bus, there were two policemen from the Herceg Novi MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you arrived at the border, did you carry on in this bus or did you switch buses?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: In the town of Pluzine we waited for an hour. A bus came from Foca and then we switched buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The bus from Foca, was it a civilian bus or a military vehicle?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: A military bus would have been painted accordingly, I guess, so this was a civilian bus but probably used by the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why do you think it was used by the military?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: The driver who drove us wore a military uniform, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who guarded you on the bus? Was there -- were there policemen or soldiers on the bus with you, except for the driver?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: There was one policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From Herceg Novi or from Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, from Foca, from Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you also have an escort in a different vehicle following or in front of the bus?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: After about 10 or 20 kilometres, a police vehicle met us and turned around and then escorted us to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those in the police car, could you see what they were wearing? Were they police or military?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I could not discern it, believe me. It was night-time already. At 7.30 or 8.00 in the evening, it's already dark. You can't see. And I sat in the middle of the bus so I couldn't really see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you arrive at the KP Dom, at what time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I arrived in the KP Dom on the 25th of May at half past nine in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I was there very long, 29 months and 16 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you arrived at the KP Dom, who received you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: We were received by a group, by a platoon, one might say, of soldiers or rather uniformed individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many soldiers were there, about?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, eight, maybe ten, at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I recognised Radomir Matovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Radomir Matovic, if you want me to tell you, (redacted) (redacted). That is number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And what was his job?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He worked in the kitchen of the KP Dom. That is, he was the chief, the head of the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he there before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, before the war, he worked in the restaurant of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And during your detention in KP Dom, was he also working there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you saw him on your arrival, was he in military uniform or did he have his kitchen clothing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He had a military uniform and had a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And these other soldiers, did you recognise anyone else or would you know which unit they were?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No. I really could not recognise those others.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you mistreated or abused on your arrival?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: As we were getting off the bus, they beat us one by one. They were lining us up against the wall of the KP Dom and would strike each one of us with the rifle butt, searching us and then kicking us and hitting us. I mean, they hit us with whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you kicked and hit?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How often were you kicked and hit?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, a number of times, but I really could not count them right then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you injured on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, logically, I felt the effects later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of effects did you feel?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: In -- around my right shoulder, and in the lower back on this side here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Does that mean you had pain in these regions or did you also have -- could one see something on the skin?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Right shoulder, on my right shoulder, one could see a bruise from the rifle butt for five or ten days. And then, of course, the pain in the rib cage and around the rib cage, and in the shoulder area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you beaten by just one soldier or by several soldiers, do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I think it was several of them. No, I don't think; I'm sure it was several of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what about the other Muslim detainees? Were they beaten as well on this occasion? Did you observe that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Same thing. Same thing. We all went through the same torture programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the soldiers say anything to you while they were beating?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. They were using expletives, dirty language.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What happened to the Serbs on the bus? Were they beaten as well?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. They took them into the KP Dom first, of course hitting them with their hands and feet and telling them, "Here you are, Serb traitors."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were they beaten as severely as the Muslims? Was it all alike?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Oh, no. Oh, no, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So what was the difference? Can you describe how they were beaten and how the Muslims were beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, those who received them in the doorway, they did not go in. They merely pushed them in by hitting them and kicking them from the back, and that is how they would enter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were regular prison guards present when this happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was present, and where were they?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: At the entrance into the KP Dom building there was Slavko Koroman, Zoran Mijovic, and Milenko Elecic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Slavko Koroman, who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Before the war he was a policeman, or rather a guard in the KP Dom. And on the eve of the war he was retired, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And during your detention?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: And during my detention I was told later on that he was hired on again as the guard commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Zoran Mijovic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Zoran Mijovic was a driver for the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he there before the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He was a driver too, and during the war I would see him drive a vehicle, but not all that often.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Milenko Elecic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Milenko Elecic was a guard before the war; and during my stay there, guard again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were they also beating the detainees or where were they?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: They were in front of the entrance, in front of the front door into the KP Dom. I've told you that. And the prisoners would go between them, would go in, passing between them. And then, when we entered, they searched us, seized our identity cards, money, jewellery, watches.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could they see from the entrance, could they see what was -- that you were beaten, being beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we could, because they were next to us, that is, next to that section of the wall where the people had been lined up.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How far from the entrance where they were did this happen, that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you were lined up and beaten? Could you say how many metres?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: From the entrance, the length - well, I don't know - fifteen metres. How much space do 21 men take?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did they do while you were being beaten? Did they react in any way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, they did not react. They somehow looked to me as a guard of honour. They did nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has just described the incident 5.4 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you handed in your identification card. Were you registered by Mr. Koroman or Elecic? Were your particulars taken down?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, they did not take down any particulars, unless they took them over from the Herceg-Novi police, because they did have an envelope with them when we were on the bus together.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see that this envelope was handed over to one of the KP Dom staff?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were you taken in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Inside the KP Dom, and then I was taken to Room 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Room 20, where was it in the building? Just the floor.

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: It was on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which of the buildings? In the left or the right wing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: The right wing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From your Room 20, could you see the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I could see the Drina River, its up-flow, where Cehotina flows into the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you see the river right in front of the KP Dom, especially the bridge over the Drina, from Room 20?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, I could not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Room 20?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: In Room 20, I was there until the 12th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many detainees were together with you in Room 20?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: In the early days, that is, when I was brought there, 21 of us were in that room for three or four days, and then some 50, up to 60 people were brought to that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From which areas did they come, these other people?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: They distributed them from other rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but from which area did they come originally? Were they from Foca or other places?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Foca and neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What ethnicity did these people have?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: They were all Muslims, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These detainees, all of the detainees in Room 20, were they all civilians or was there a soldier among you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Not a single soldier was there among them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were sick people among you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: In Room 20, Esad Hadzic was the most serious case at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did he have?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He had an ulcer. He was an ulcer patient from before. However, during a day or two, he still had medicines he had been issued in Ulcinj.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were the medicines --

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: And when he used the medicines all up, then he began to feel pain. His ulcer burst on the 6th or the 8th of June, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he inform the guards that he needed medicine?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, as he was running short of medicines, of course, he was -- he tried to prepare himself for this and, yes, he did ask for medicines, but to no avail.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When he asked for medicines, did you see how the guards reacted to this request?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Since he was really very ill, he simply could not stand up any more, so we risked on his behalf -- we opened the window, and asked the guard to help, to either take them -- take him somewhere or come to the room and help him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall which guard was addressed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic was in the compound yard. Then when people came to the window to inform him, they called to him, "Guard, guard," and he pointed the rifle at them and shouted, "Shut the window or I'll shoot." And we had to obey the orders, and so we shut the window.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Hadzic died on the 8th of June. How did he die?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Sometime on the 6th, his ulcer perforated and he bled intensively. He ran a high fever. We applied cold compresses and gave him water to drink all the time. And then on the 7th of July, a male nurse came to see him, realised that nothing would come out of him, and then they took him to the clinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, he said "July" there. I'm not sure that was intended.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said "July." Is it June or July?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: June, June, definitely, June.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And you said he was taken to the clinic. Do you mean the hospital -- Foca hospital or what clinic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: The clinic in the KP Dom compound, the surgery.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said he died. Where did he die?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He died in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Foca hospital or the clinic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: In the Foca hospital, in the hospital in Foca. He died the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: His uncle Hadzic was with me in the same room, his father's brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And how did Mr. Hadzic get this information that he had died?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Because he went with him to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how did you learn that he died? Did Mr. Hadzic, the uncle, tell you when he returned? Or how?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, natural, I learned it from Munib Hadzic who came back and he said, "Nothing will -- nothing will come out of him," and he brought along a jacket or something that he had with him. And from him it is that I learned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were you taken after the 12th of June?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I was taken to Room 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in -- where was Room 11?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Room 11 was on the ground floor of the left wing of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did you have to switch to this Room 11, do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I don't -- I didn't know it then and I don't understand it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Room 11?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: In Room 11, I stayed, I think, until the 18th, maybe 19th -- 18th of July, July.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many detainees were together with you in Room 11?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Seventy-two.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how can -- did you know them from before, these 72?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, most of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what ethnicity did these detainees have in Room 11?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: In Room 11, of 72 detainees, two were Croats, Mate Ivancic and Kruno Marinovic, and the rest were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were sick people among those 72?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned the Serbs arrested in Montenegro. How long did they stay in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I saw them for three or four days, not longer than that. I mean, in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know what became out of them? Did you see them being taken away?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: They were taken away at night so that I could not see that, but my guess is that they were taken to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Besides them, were other Serb prisoners detained in the KP Dom, during your detention time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were they kept? Were they kept separate?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. They were kept in the right wing of the building, Room 21 or whatever they were called, in that building, and above Room 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see them in the compound?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were they soldiers or civilians? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Most of them had uniforms, military uniforms, on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to clarify something in relation to the detainees in Room 11. You said that there were no sick people among you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: In Room 11, I found some sick people. I found, and yes, there were some people who were ill in Room 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you recall who was ill?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I remember Mujo Murguz, Ibrahim Ovcina, Hamdija Mandzo, Aziz Sahinovic, Ismet Pasovic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And let me just go from one to the other. Mujo Murguz, what did -- what kind of sickness did he have?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He was a mental case simply. Very -- a man very tense, aggressive. I mean, I am not a specialist but those were the signs, the visible signs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did he get treatment for his mental condition?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, no. He was not treated.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What became out of him? Was he released from the KP Dom, do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I think he was taken for exchange once, but one does not -- it is not known if it ever took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean he's missing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: It does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how do you know that? Did you have contacts with his family? Or how did you find out that he's missing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: From the family, and acquaintances, and the survivors from the camp, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you mentioned Ibrahim Ovcina, what did he suffer from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He also had psychological problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you observe anything particular?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, when you see a man eat a cake of soap, you can see for yourself what state of health -- what his state of health is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what became of him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He was also taken for exchange, and all trace of him was lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know these two persons from before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I did know Ibrahim Ovcina, because he had also come from the teachers school and we were peers. We were all of the same generation. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he mentally disturbed before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, never, as far as I know, not before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before we leave, is it going to be necessary to sign a redaction form for that reference to his occupation?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. He said that he was a teacher from the beginning, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did he?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. There is no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You told him to not to say what he was doing, and I had thought he had complied with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. The position that he had, not his profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right, then. My recollection has been refreshed, by looking at the transcript, as to Mr. Bakrac's problems with Witness FWS-05. That discussion arose when you had Witness 182 here, and you tendered an exit permit in the name of Witness 05. It was made very clear at the time that that was no evidence in relation to Witness 05. It was just the form of document that we were interested in, and that it would be no evidence at all in relation to any exit permit being granted to Witness 05. If that's the problem, I don't know whether it still exists, but when you speak to Mr. Bakrac about 05, there was a very clear reference to this. It is at page 1610 of the transcript. And I think that that may resolve the problem between you. If there is some other problem, we will have to deal with it at some later stage. We will adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, before the break we spoke about those in Room 11 that were sick, and you mentioned Hamdija Mandzo. What did he -- what kind of sickness did he have?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Hamdija Mandzo, I know from before the war that he was a tuberculosis patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did the living conditions at KP Dom affect his health? Did you see anything? Did you notice?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Absolutely. The shortage of food and of basic hygienic conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in which way did his health deteriorate? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I could see his weakness. For some time he was bedridden; he couldn't even get up.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did he survive the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He was exchanged. He survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, I know from quite a few citizens who saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You also mentioned Ismet Pasovic. What did he suffer from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Ismet Pasovic, before the war he was also a serious heart patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did the living conditions in KP Dom affect his health condition?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: A shortage of medicine, absolutely, which he probably had to use all the time; also poor nutrition, psychological problems. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know what became of him? Did he survive?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I know that he did not survive.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that? What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I know that he was taken away in a group of 23 inmates towards Montenegro, towards the town of Pluzine, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: And that group of people had never been exchanged, nor do I know of them being alive at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you speak with his relatives, or how do you know that he is missing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I know because his wife called me personally. She asked. Also his friends, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I forgot to ask you in relation to Mr. Ovcina, Ibrahim Ovcina. How do you know that he disappeared? Did you speak with relatives or how do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Ibrahim's family asked me about what had happened to him, how come he disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned Aziz Sahinovic. What did he suffer from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Aziz Sahinovic, he had a bad psychosis. He was a psychiatric patient, basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how did you see that? What did you see him do that you saw that he has a psychosis?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: When I came to Room 11, Aziz Sahinovic's bed was opposite my bed. During the first few days I came to the conclusion that the man was not doing well, that he was gone, psychologically speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? Could he not talk to you properly, or what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: That too, yes, normal conversation. And also his behaviour. He's a man I knew before the war, and then I saw for myself what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just want to clarify one point. You said that in the Room 20, you were -- the group of you, the 21 from Montenegro and some 50 or 60 more, and you said in Room 11, you were 72 people. But do you recall that you gave previous statements to the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I said, and I think that that is right, the 21 persons stayed in that room for three or four days and then later, when everyone was relocated from other rooms as well, then this room was filled up, in the sense that it reached the number that I had mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I just want to clarify: 72, you mentioned the number of 72. Were there 72 in the Room 11 or in the Room 20?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Maybe there has been a confusion of numbers. I'm sure that in Room 11, there were 72 persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, we do not need to go into the details of the living conditions. That was done with other witnesses. But I would like to know from you, do you know if the living conditions, especially the food rations, were deliberately kept so low?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. This was done deliberately, all of this that had to do with meals.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I know, in that period, and perhaps a year before that, there was enough food in the area of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that? What do you mean? Were there food reserves?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Absolutely. All military reserves, flour, food, all of that was in the hands of the people of Foca, the town of Foca and the people who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to the -- what became of the food reserves? Who used them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Absolutely, it was the Serb population of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is that your conclusion or did you see anything related to that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: It is primarily my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see the food that was available to the staff?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: You mean the staff who were detained or the staff who was doing the serving? You mean the personnel who were doing the serving?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The staff of the KP Dom. Did you see if they had food available to them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: They had much better food. Actually, they had normal meals. They were not in a situation to eat what we had to eat or what we could eat, or rather which we had to eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how do you know that? Did you actually see them eat in the canteen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I saw it and, absolutely, our people who worked in the kitchen could tell us about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know -- did you observe food deliveries arriving in KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you -- when did you observe that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Once I had the opportunity. It was in August, July or August, when a truck full of food arrived from Titovo Uzice. Actually, the truck had licence plates of Titovo Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say August or July, what year?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what happened when the food-- the truck arrived? Was it unloaded? And who did that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I personally unloaded it. Vujicic was the man who worked at the warehouse. There was sugar, marmalade, pasta, salt, oil. That's what was there then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said you personally unloaded it. Who ordered you to unload it and where did you have to take it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I was ordered by one of the guards. I can't remember now which one it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where did you -- where was the food then stored, these deliveries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: It was stored at the warehouse, that is by the stairs that lead to the dining room where we had our lunch, our meals.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did the detainees get this food? You mentioned some of the food deliveries. Did the detainees get it, do you know, at least parts of it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: As for what I had unloaded, we never got any such thing on our table.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall that a TV crew once entered the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I don't know whether my time is going to be very accurate now. It was July, I think. I don't know about the date for sure. A CNN crew came.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "July," what year?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know in advance that a TV crew was coming or was it a surprise when they came?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I did not know. It was a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the KP Dom look different on that day when the crew was there, the TV crew, or was it like usual?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, the room where I was then, Room 11, was not any different.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know about the other rooms?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I don't know, because the crew came from the right part of the building, and I don't know whether they had been to see some other rooms. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you get -- on this day, did you get the same amount of food or was it different?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, look. I have to clarify something. What happened was that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a TV crew came twice, or rather one crew and one TV crew. And now I'm just saying that I saw a TV crew of CNN that came to a place underneath my windows. And the crew that came to see the canteen and probably to film whatever was going on there, normal life or -- whether it was normal or not, that's a different question, but that was a different crew.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was this other crew there, this different one?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: This crew came sometime around the beginning of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where did they come from? From which station?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, it's not a TV station. This is a crew headed by Mr. Mitar Rasevic. They simply happened to come as we were having lunch.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So you mean it was just journalists, a delegation of journalists, or what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I don't know what delegation this was or whatever. I just know that the lunch was a bit more festive that day, or rather the meals were a bit more plentiful.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On that second occasion in August 1992 or on the first occasion? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the KP Dom staff prepare in any way for this second crew to come in?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, we who were detained there carried out preparations for about a day or two. We were ordered to clean all the premises: the kitchen, the rooms, the compound, the yard. That was it.
