utterances.text: Did you recognise any other persons in the room, any others who joined in -- were involved in the beating?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, although other persons told me about others, but I do not accept that unless I've seen it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see the victims, or one of them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I could see Halim Konjo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what was he doing? Was he standing? Was he lying? What could you see?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He was standing, and he had a cut up here in this part of the head, because you could see traces of blood on the yellow T-shirt that he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was pointing at the left side -- left back side of his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it was of his neck more.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Down here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Oh, yes, absolutely, yes, the upper part of the neck.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any of the victims leave the room after the beating?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, after the beating, of course they left the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But could you see how that happened? How -- in which condition they left the room? Could they walk on their own or how?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I doubt they could walk on their own feet. They were mistreated and beaten so badly that I really doubted that any one of them could have stood on his own two feet, let alone walked on his own.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The question is: Did you personally see them leave the room, in whatever manner?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No. I personally did not see them, but I assume, because I saw when the blankets were thrown in, the door was open, and two men appeared, quite unknown to me. I could not recognise them. They left the blankets by the wall and they withdrew through the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At what point in time were blankets thrown into the room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: The blankets were thrown in sometime after the second beating, after the beating of Nurko Nisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How were the conditions in regard of the light when this happened? Was the light in the room? Was it still daylight? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I already started that this began around 6.00 or 7.00 and during the first beatings, it is natural to have daylight, say, by 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when, as the evening progressed, was there light in the room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, there was, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether the translation was right but the question was: Was there still light in the room? And if I understood the witness correctly, he said that this started around 6.00 or 7.00, and that there would be daylight until 9.00. He didn't say that there was light in the room. He said that there was daylight until 9.00. And then the Prosecutor asks after that, since there was light in the room, et cetera, in the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I think that the week off has given you greater impetus in taking minute points. The evidence goes this way: "How were the conditions in relation -- in regard of the light when this happened? Was the light in the room? Was it still daylight? Do you recall that?" Then the witness answered: "I already stated that this began around 6.00 or 7.00, and during the first beatings it is natural to have daylight, say, by 9.00." Then the next question was: "And when, as the evening progressed, was there light in the room?" Not "still light"; "was there light?" What's wrong with that? It's not a leading question. It's a perfectly normal question. It's not contradictory to anything he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the translation I got, because I'm following the interpretation here, I got that kind of translation and I reacted in order to be able to respond as soon as possible, but I didn't manage to look at the transcript and to see what the transcript said. I heard the interpreter say, "Was there still light in the room?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: At this stage, I'm afraid, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I have no recollection of what you did say, but the translation looked perfectly correct - I'm sorry - the transcript looked perfectly correct to me when the objection was first taken. Did you say "still"?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. I said a light, because I was actually referring to other sources of light, like electricity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's what I thought you were meaning too. Well, Mr. Bakrac, I think that you -- if that's the interpretation you got, well, then, your objection was fair enough, but the translation itself was clearly wrong. There was no reference to "still." My reaction to the question was "electric light," and that's clearly what she's after. So your objection is overruled, and I'm sorry that you were misled by the translation you received, if that was indeed what was said. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. You proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was electric light in the room after darkness had fallen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, no, there was no electric light.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there any other source of light in the room after it was dark, after 9.00?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: A torch light was used; a gas torch light, actually, was used in order to give light.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the window, was the window open?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: The window was broken. There was an ordinary wooden board that was -- that covered half of where the window pane was supposed to be, so the window was half open.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever enter this room you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in the month of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did you enter this room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I entered the room because I was told to clean part of the hallway with Mujo Dudic, another inmate, and all the other rooms along there, and I had this ugly honour of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did the room look like when you had to clean it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, there were traces of dried blood on the floor and on the walls, and I found a few wooden batons and a metal one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did these tools, this metal one and the wooden batons -- did you see anything on them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, on the wooden batons I could see that there was blood.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know when, approximately when you cleaned the room, when in August? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I think it was around the 8th of August, I think. I have it written down, but I think it's the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have mentioned -- you have named several persons that were taken on that occasion. Do you know what happened to these people? Did any of them ever appear again? Were any of them ever seen alive?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, none of them have ever been seen alive since.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you in contact with any of the relatives of these people, or even all of them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, I did not really have an opportunity of being in contact Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with all of them, but with most of them I did have contact: relatives, family, people like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have contact with the family of Nurko Nisic, and what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, I had contact with his wife directly and his daughter. They were inquiring as to whether I knew anything about him. It was hard for me to tell them what I saw and what I knew about Nurko.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Halim Konjo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. Halim Konjo's wife also called me, and his daughter-in-law or sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that it's an ambiguous word.

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I said that -- I told them what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment. The interpreter has drawn our attention to a problem we have had before about the ambiguity in the B/C/S language about in-laws.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This word is snaha, s-n-a-h-a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is it the daughter-in-law or the sister-in-law? How were they related?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Sister-in-law. His brother's wife. When I say "snaha," I'm referring to his brother's wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Nail Hodzic, did you have any contact with Nail Hodzic's relatives?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We've lost the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The usher had better press the microphone again. One moment. No, no. He obviously knocked the button. I've done it myself, to the horror of the interpreters. It was the button that was pressed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with the relatives of the Rikalo brothers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, none with them, because I have no idea where his relatives are or what they are doing. Or rather, I once spoke to his father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Whose father-in-law? Which of the Rikalos?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Husein's.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Kuloglija Mustafa, did you contact the relatives or did they contact you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No. No, I did not communicate with his family, with his relatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Krunoslav Marinovic's family?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, I do not know his relatives. He was married to a woman from Foca, but I don't know his family.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Esad Kiselica?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk to Esad Kiselica's wife.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are they still missing, do you know, from your contacts? Are they still missing? Were their bodies ever found?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, they have not, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that several groups were taken away. When was the next group taken away? Between the incident that you just described, when was the next group taken out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: It was four or five days later, at intervals of four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many were called out on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Nine again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you recall who was called out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Seval Soro, Mate Ivancic, Zulfo Veiz, Ekrem Tulek, Mandzo -- no, not Mandzo. Cankusic, Refik. I'm not sure I can remember all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that Husein Rikalo was in this second group. You told that already in your testimony today and you have already said who he is. Zulfo Veiz, who is that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Zulfo Veiz was a policeman in the former police station in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he in Room 11 when he was taken out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know in which room he was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I think he was in Room 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you mentioned Mate Ivancic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Zulfo Veiz, Your Honour, I forgot to say, is C-29 and 5.27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Mate Ivancic was a medical technician, a laboratory assistant. He worked in the hospital, a Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "a Catholic," does that mean a Croat?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, his ethnicity, yes. Yes, yes, a Croat, a Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was he in Room 11?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's C-11.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned Refik Cankusic, that's C-4. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I know his elder brother and his father better than I know him. I know he was trained as a locksmith, but that is about all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned Soro Seval. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Seval Soro was an electrician and he worked at Electrodistribucija Foca, that is, power distribution company in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I forgot to ask you, Refik Cankusic, was he in your room, in Room 11, or was he somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No. He was in Room 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Soro Seval, was he in Room 11?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Soro Seval was with me in 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's the person C-24.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You also mentioned a Tulek. Who was he? Tulek, Kemal, who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Kemal Tulek was a guard in the KP Dom before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was he in your room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, no, he was not with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This person is C-25.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a Bico Hamid, nicknamed Salem?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I think it's a mistake. There is no Hamid Bico. His name is Salem Bico.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who is he? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: He was a policeman in Foca for a while, and then two or three years before the war, he started his own cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he in your room, in Room 11, or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, no. He wasn't in my room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is C-2 and B-5.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was Salem Bico in this group of people who were taken as the second group, or was he in any of the groups?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was in the second group.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a Vahida Dzemal?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Dzemal Vahida was also a policeman in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was he also taken away in one of the groups, and if so, in which; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I think he was with a third group, with Altoka. I think it was the third group.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was he in Room 11?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was in my dormitory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already mentioned Fuad Mandzo. In which -- was he also taken away in that manner and, if so, in which group?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. Fuad Mandzo left with the third group.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Fuad Mandzo, that's C-16.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When this second group was led away, were they -- what happened to -- what did you see happen to them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, I became too afraid to look through the window, as I did in the first group's case. I simply -- my nerves were frayed and I dared not look at him any more because those screams that reached us were horrible, same beatings, same torture.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see these people line up in front of the metal door?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely, same treatment as the first group, except that I wasn't at the window to watch directly what went on. But I would cast a look now and then and see people going in or coming out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you -- you mentioned that -- when you described to us Refik Cankusic, you mentioned his father. Was his father also in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes. His father was in the same room with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When his son Refik was taken away, how did this affect the father?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: His father had a heart condition from before the war, so he fell into a coma and we had serious problems with him because we had no experience with -- we did not know how to help him. We did not have any tablets that could help him. So for two or three hours, we really had a lot of problems until we managed to bring him back, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did he fall in a coma?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, when Refik was taken inside - and before that, he had heard the screams of others - he naturally assumed that the same thing would happen to his son, and simply he, I suppose, did not have enough strength, enough courage, to listen to this, and he simply collapsed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: After this second group had been beaten, did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: The second group was beaten in the same area that I described in the first case, so I absolutely heard it. I absolutely could not sleep until it went on. And it went on until late into the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And after the beating had stopped, did you hear anything else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Same procedure. One shot, as many shots as the number of persons. And again, the same sounds of a truck unloading in front of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's -- did you hear of any of these people you just mentioned? Did you hear from them again or was anybody found, or the bodies of any of the victims?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about that yet. I heard about one victim, and that was the body -- I forgot to say that. It was Halim Konjo's body.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how did you hear this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, I heard it from my sister's daughter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were you in contact of the family -- of any family members of this group of victims that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, of them, I communicated with Salem Bico's family, Zulfo Veiz's. And with others, no, I did not. I didn't have an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You've already mentioned the third group, and that Vahida Dzemal and Mandzo Fuad belonged to this third group. When were they taken away? How much time elapsed between second group and third group?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: The third group was taken three or four days after the second Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. group.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you recall who, besides Mandzo Fuad and Vahida Dzemal, was in this group?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I remember two Altokas, but I don't know the first name of the other one. I can't remember it, that is. Nermin Hadzimusic, Adil Krajcin, Enes Uzunovic, Ismet Karahasanovic, and Suad Sulabasic [phoen] -- No, excuse me. He was in the fourth group.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would it help you to look into your notes or can you -- can we continue like we do now? Is it --

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, it would go much quicker if I could look at my notes, at least some of the names that you are asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before we do that, I would have to ask you some questions. When did you make the notes?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: In KP Dom, I kept my private diary, and when I was exchanged, the diary was taken away from me and it was about a thousand pages long. However, yes, I'd really like -- I miss that document. I'd really like to have it. Now, when I arrived here -- well, not the first day, but when I left during the first month, I just jotted down something so as not to forget the events, things that happened to me and others, and I had those notes. Of course, it was all handwritten. And later on, I typed some of it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the handwritten notes -- the notes that you have with you today are typed notes, the typed notes or the handwritten ones?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: They are typed on a typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did you type it? You said first you had handwritten notes, but when did you type them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, I did it perhaps two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you made these typed notes -- were all the dates and all the names in your notes, are they from your memory or the events? Is it your personal memory or did someone help you make your notes?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: I primarily relied on my memory, and also, when I communicated with other people, they helped, because we searched and found the dates that were interesting and correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. It's not clear, to me, at least, when the first handwritten notes, of which these are the typed copy, were compiled. He said after he'd first been here. I assume that's when he was first interviewed by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. I understood -- but we can clarify it. I actually understood that he made them the first month after his release, but we have to find out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you make the first handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: The first notes I put down in 1994, in December, and I was in the place that I am living now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why did you make the handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Well, I realised that I might need them sometime, and simply to write down something so that generations to come would know what happened to me and my people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These handwritten notes, did they base on your memory only or did you already consult?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think he's made that clear, that where he couldn't remember something, he spoke to other people, and it's a collective record -- sorry, it's a record of a collective memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I understand that to be right for the typed notes. I was wondering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I shouldn't have interfered. Reading the transcript, it seemed reasonably clear, but if it's not clear to you, then we had better get it straight.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: To me, it was not clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The handwritten notes, did they base on your memory, or was it also already after consultation with other people?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: My personal memory, my memories from the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you made the typed notes, you said that it is the collective memory, you consulted others. Whom did you consult?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: With people who were in the camp with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The witness had shown us this document and we have made copies, but of course they are in B/C/S. We didn't have an opportunity to read it or translate it. It's just for his -- for helping him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, he needs to see them, and Mr. Bakrac needs to see them. He can read B/C/S, so it seems to be perfectly appropriate we should proceed. But you had better, I think, have the document marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: A copy for the translation booth as well. That document -- yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, with your leave, the Defence does have an objection. We're against reading this document because we were given a typed document. We do not know where is that handwritten document on the basis of which we could verify its authenticity. All we have here is a typed document which is the product of collective memory, as he explained to us, and we object against using such a typed document during this witness' testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you objecting simply because the handwritten notes made after he had been released have not been produced or are you objecting generally?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we saw here notes which accompanied some of the exhibits which the witnesses had written, and we did not object against them. But the statements of this witness did not have any notes as an annex or something. All we were given were sketches, were his drawings, the drawings of the KP Dom done in his hand. Now, the question arises: If he had those sketches, then he must have had also those handwritten notes. This is the first time we are given a document which was typewritten, which was typed, and its source could be questionable, to say the least. Besides, the witness says that the handwritten document was the product of collective memory, what he also discussed with other people and what he knew himself, and that was what he wrote down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see no point in the second part of the objection, but I still want to get a yes or a no answer. Is the basis of your objection that he has not produced the handwritten notes that he wrote himself after he was released, or is it to any assistance to his memory at all that you are objecting?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my objection is that his notes have not been produced in evidence, his handwritten notes which he wrote himself after he left the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I be given the floor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment, sir. All right. Now I understand it. Now, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you will have to tell us at least what's happened to the handwritten notes. Their absence may not be fatal, but we've got to know what's happened to them, because they are obviously an earlier version, of which the typed version is not just a typed copy of them but with additional material.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we actually have to ask the witness, because we did not see the notes, the handwritten notes, and not the typed notes either, so I have to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Nevertheless, there is a gap in the description of how these typed notes came into existence, so I suggest you ask that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where are the handwritten notes? Do you have your handwritten notes with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: No, I don't have them here. I have them at home, where I live now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why did you make these typed notes?

utterances.speaker: FWS-71
utterances.text: Because I didn't put the sequence of events all right and my handwriting is not very legible. And what I wrote here, this is all taken from my notes, all just the way that I did it in my handwritten notes, except that I consulted some people who were -- who had been with me as regards the dates. So the only question here which could arise is dates, which I complemented here, I mean complementing the notes which I had written by hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you now know the course in which it's come out. You maintain your objection, I assume, on the basis that the handwritten notes are not produced. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does that not just go to the weight of them rather than the right of the witness or the permission that could be granted to the witness to refresh his recollection from this document? The document itself is not being tendered; he is simply being asked whether he would like to refresh his recollection as to certain dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are quite right, and I agree, and I fully trust the Chamber and their ability to assess the weight, but the Defence could not but raise objection. I also think that this brings into question the probative value of the testimony. And the Defence is satisfied, but I thought it my duty to object to this form of testimony, because I also think it is a contribution to the evaluation of the probative value of this witness' testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The document will be marked for identification 6. Now, if I may say so, Mr. Bakrac, if only to make you feel happy, if in a common-law country a witness had said he wanted to refresh his recollection from notes, the cross-examiner would not be permitted to see that document unless he undertook to tender it in evidence, so the fact that you're being given a copy of it gives you a great advantage over what you would have got from anywhere else. Nevertheless, we understand, I can assure you, that the weight to be given to the witness' evidence will depend to some extent upon our view about this document, if the dates become of importance. Now, before we adjourn, I should tell you that next Tuesday, that's the 20th, tomorrow a week, the judgement of the Appeals Chamber in the Celebici case is being given, and I have to be there because I was the Presiding Judge in the Appeals Chamber, and it is being delivered at 3.30 next Tuesday afternoon. Bearing in mind that there are a number of accused to be brought in and there is going to be some degree of public interest in the proceedings, it does not seem as if we will be able to sit that afternoon. So from the point of view of what witnesses you bring next Tuesday, you may assume we will not be sitting on Tuesday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now till 9.30 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of February, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 24 25
